about.title: A Bit About Me
about.sub: From shipping games to shipping insights.
about.pivot_text: I spent three years as a mobile game developer across three studios: Mirabo, Wingsmob (spun off from Inwave Studio), and Zitga. I worked on gameplay code, live-ops, and player-retention metrics. At Zitga I shipped 5 games to Google Play. Chasing those retention numbers is what pulled me toward data: I wanted to understand the "why" behind the charts, not just watch them move. So I switched lanes into data analysis full-time.
about.think_text: I approach problems the way I designed game systems — find the feedback loop, measure what changes behaviour, cut what doesn't move the needle. Theory of Fun put words to it: learning IS the fun. Data analysis is the same thing with a different dataset.

p1.sub: A game developer picks his next data role — with data. Five careers compared side by side on pay, entry barriers, switching cost and skill ROI, across 1.6M job postings (2023–2025).
p1.s1_sub: Median pay with P25–P75 spread, and who's actually hiring — 5 roles, 2023–2025
p1.chart_salary_sub: USD/year · band = middle 50% of salaries (P25–P75), tick = median
p1.s2_title: Which role is easiest to enter?
p1.s2_sub: Junior-posting share, degree requirements, and the degree penalty — controlled for seniority
p1.chart_degpen_sub: mid-level median pay · ● no degree mentioned · ○ degree required
p1.s3_sub: Skill-set overlap between roles — Jaccard similarity of each role's top-15 skills
p1.s1_insight: Data Engineer leads on pay ($125K mid-level median) but Data Scientist has the widest spread — high ceiling, high variance. Data Analyst pays least ($88K) yet posts the most jobs of any role. Pay and demand point at different winners — which is exactly why one chart was never enough.
p1.s2_insight: Data Analyst is the easiest role to enter: 7.6% junior share (double Data Engineer's), a typical ask of just 3 skills (DE asks 6), and near-zero degree penalty (−$0.4K). Skipping a degree costs a mid-level Data Scientist $25K/year; it costs a Data Analyst almost nothing.
p1.confounder_note: How to read this: each row compares typical pay for the same role at the same career level — postings that require a degree (○) vs postings that don't (●). The line between the dots is what skipping a degree costs; two dots on the same spot (Data Engineer) mean a degree changes nothing. Why compare only same-level jobs? Senior postings pay more and skip degree requirements more often — mixing levels made no-degree Software Engineers look +$22K richer. Same-level comparison flips it to the real −$25K.
p1.s3_insight: Data Analyst and Business Analyst overlap at 0.88 — effectively one job with two titles. DA→DS costs a moderate re-skill (0.43); DA→DE is nearly a restart (0.20). For someone coming from software, DE is SE's closest match (0.30) — the engineering habits transfer.
p1.s4_title: Which skill should a Data Analyst learn next?
p1.s4_sub: Salary premium vs demand, inside mid-level DA postings only (level-controlled)
p1.chart_roi_sub: x = % of DA postings asking for it · y = median salary lift
p1.chart_features_sub: Permutation importance · green = higher pay, red = lower
p1.s4_insight: Python adds +$12K to a mid-level DA salary and appears in a third of postings — the clear next bet. Cloud skills (AWS/Azure) pay well but are asked for less often; Excel is demanded everywhere and pays a negative premium. Learn what's scarce-but-paid, not what's everywhere.
p1.ml_note: How it works: A gradient-boosted model (HistGradientBoosting, which beat Linear, Ridge and Random Forest in 5-fold cross-validation) is trained on 79 features from US postings only — binary skill flags (SQL, Python, Spark…), how many skills each posting lists, an ordinal seniority level parsed from the raw job title, the job role, the top-10 hiring states, and a few extras (remote, health insurance, degree-optional). Permutation importance measures how much R² drops when each feature is shuffled. Green bars push a posting toward a higher salary; red toward lower. R² = 0.53 means these features explain a little over half of US salary variance — the rest is structurally invisible because exact years of experience, the specific employer, and total comp/equity are not columns in this dataset.
p1.s5_title: Does a machine learning model agree with the charts?
p1.s5_sub: Gradient-boosted regression · US annual salary from seniority, role, skills & state
p1.s5_insight: The model independently confirms the comparison: seniority explains 47% of predictable salary variance — more than any skill — and the 'Data Analyst' flag is the single biggest negative driver. Translation: the ladder you pick matters more than the tools you list, which is exactly what the role comparison showed.
p1.s6_sub: Local postings reverse the global ranking — with honest sample sizes
p1.vn_caveat: Only 3,770 of 1.6M postings are Vietnam-based — and just 145 for Business Analyst. Too thin for salary math (so we don't chart it), but the demand ranking is clear: Data Engineer leads Vietnam while Data Analyst leads globally. Aggregate data misleads; check your own market.
p1.s7_sub: Six criteria, five roles, one honest answer
p1.s7_insight: Two-step verdict: Data Analyst is the entry point — highest junior share, near-zero degree penalty (−$0.4K), 3-skill ask, and an 0.88 overlap with BA as a free fallback. Data Engineer is the growth destination — top mid-level pay, #1 in Vietnam, and the strongest skill bridge back to software engineering. Enter as an analyst; grow toward the pipeline.

p2.sub: Analysed an A/B test from the mobile game Cookie Cats (90,189 players) to determine whether moving the first gate from level 30 to level 40 affects player retention. Applied chi-square tests and bootstrap analysis to validate results.
p2.s1_title: How was the experiment set up?
p2.s1_sub: Random assignment of players into two groups
p2.s2_title: Does gate placement change who comes back?
p2.s2_sub: 1-day and 7-day retention rates by gate position
p2.s3_title: Is the difference real, or just luck?
p2.s3_sub: 1,000 bootstrap iterations — distribution of retention difference
p2.s4_title: Does the gate change how much people play?
p2.s4_sub: Total rounds played per group — player engagement patterns
p2.s1_insight: 44,700 players in Gate 30, 45,489 in Gate 40 — a near-perfect split that eliminates sampling as an explanation for any difference found.
p2.s2_insight: Gate 30 wins on 7-day retention: 19.02% vs 18.20%, and the gap is statistically significant (p = 0.0016). The 1-day gap is smaller and doesn’t clear the significance bar.
p2.s3_insight: The entire bootstrap distribution clears zero — the 95% CI is [+0.34%, +1.28%]. Not noise. Gate 30 consistently outperforms Gate 40 across 1,000 resamples.
p2.note_retention: Reading these bars: each is the return rate within its own group (players who came back ÷ that group’s size), so the two don’t add to 100% — they’re independent rates being compared, not a shared split. Whether the gap is real is tested with a chi-square test on the underlying player counts (a 2×2 table, df = 1): day-1 p = 0.0755 (not significant — a gap this size occurs ~7.5% of the time by chance), day-7 p = 0.0016 (significant — under ~0.2%).
p2.note_bootstrap: What the bootstrap does: the Gate 30 − Gate 40 difference is recomputed on thousands of resamples of the players (drawn with replacement), producing the distribution above. The 95% confidence interval [+0.34, +1.28 pp] is simply the middle 95% of that cloud. Because the whole interval sits to the right of the dashed zero line, the day-7 advantage holds up under resampling — it’s consistent, not an artefact of one random split.
p2.s4_insight: Both groups play roughly the same number of rounds — the gate doesn’t change how much people play, only whether they come back.
p2.conclusion_text: Keep the gate at level 30. The 7-day retention lift is statistically significant (p = 0.0016), confirmed by bootstrap, and comes at zero cost to engagement volume. Moving to level 40 only loses players long-term.

p3.sub: Not every customer is worth the same. I segmented 4,372 customers from 541,909 transactions of a UK online retailer and found the top group averages 22× the revenue of the bottom one. Here is who to keep, who to win back, and what each is worth.
p3.s1_title: Where does the revenue come from?
p3.s1_sub: Monthly revenue trend and geographic distribution
p3.s2_sub: Customer segments based on Recency, Frequency, and Monetary value
p3.s3_sub: Monthly cohort retention rates — tracking customer return behaviour
p3.chart_cohort_sub: % of customers returning each month after first purchase
p3.s4_title: So what should the business do next?
p3.s4_sub: Data-driven strategies to improve customer retention and revenue
p3.s1_insight: Revenue spikes hard in Q4 — November alone hit £1.46M. The UK drives 82% of total revenue, a concentration risk that one bad market quarter could hit hard.
p3.s2_insight: Champions (14.5% of customers) average £6,820 revenue vs £310 for Lost — a 22× gap. The 1,040 Hibernating customers are the highest-leverage win-back target right now.
p3.s3_insight: The Dec 2010 cohort retains at 36–41% monthly — every cohort after drops off noticeably. Holiday buyers are inherently higher-intent; the goal is recreating that acquisition quality outside Q4.
recs_items: Lock in your Champions (632 customers) with a loyalty tier — they’re 14.5% of your base but your highest-revenue segment.
Run a win-back campaign on 593 At-Risk customers now — personalised offers before they go fully dormant.
Grow Netherlands and Germany — strong demand, but together they’re only ~5.8% of revenue. Localised marketing is a cheap unlock.
Reverse-engineer the Dec 2010 cohort — 36–41% monthly retention is exceptional. Find out what made them stick and replicate it.

p4.sub: The pipeline underneath Project 01. Four CSVs land from Google Cloud Storage, 1.6M job postings load into DuckDB, and four analytical marts get built on top so the same questions stop needing the same joins rewritten every time.
p4.s1_title: Why not just query the CSVs?
p4.s1_sub: What modelling buys you, and what it costs.
p4.s1_insight: Four CSVs answer one question at a time. Every new question meant rewriting the same joins across 1.6M rows, and each one had a different grain: per posting, per skill per month, per company per month. Modelling it once into four marts turned each new question into a filter instead of a rewrite.
p4.s2_title: What does the star schema look like?
p4.s2_sub: Source tables in, marts out, one grain each.
p4.s2_insight: One fact table per grain, with dimensions shared where they repeat. company_mart is the widest at 8 tables because company, location and job title each needed their own dimension, plus a bridge table for the many-to-many between short job titles and full ones.
p4.s3_title: What happens when new data arrives?
p4.s3_sub: One mart updates in place. Three rebuild.
p4.grain_skills_mart: One row per skill per month
p4.grain_company_mart: One row per company per month
p4.sql_merge_title: The one mart that updates in place
p4.s3_insight: Only priority_mart refreshes incrementally, and the reason is in its schema. priority_jobs_snapshot carries an updated_at column, and the MERGE only touches rows whose priority level actually changed, so that timestamp records when a role changed rather than when the pipeline last ran. A full rebuild would stamp every row identically and throw that away. The other three marts hold no state a rebuild would destroy, so they rebuild. Incremental logic earns its complexity when a reload would lose information, which here is true exactly once.

p5.sub: {{n}} Hanoi restaurants from ShopeeFood's delivery listing, matched against their written reviews on Foody. Does the platform star rating and the review score actually agree on which restaurants are good?
p5.kpi_restaurants_sub: in the promoted, deliverable-to-one-address slice of ShopeeFood Hanoi
p5.kpi_share45_sub: of the {{n}} restaurants with enough ratings to compare
p5.kpi_correlation: correlation between the star rating and the review score
p5.kpi_correlation_sub: 0 means no agreement, 1 means the two always move together
p5.chart_rating_wall_sub: count of restaurants at each star rating · highlighted bars are 4.5 stars and above
p5.s2_sub: Median delivery price against median star rating, by restaurant category
p5.chart_price_rating_sub: bars = median price (left axis, VND) · line = median star rating (right axis, fixed to 4–5 stars)
p5.s2_insight: Median price ranges {{spread}}× across categories — from street food up to full restaurants — while the median rating moves only {{ratingSpread}} stars total, and it moves in the opposite direction: the cheaper categories rate slightly higher. Price is not what these stars are measuring.
p5.s3_title: Do the two rating systems agree?
p5.s3_sub: ShopeeFood star rating against the average Foody review score, for restaurants with both
p5.s3_insight: The same restaurant can hold a {{sf}}-star listing and a review average of {{foody}} out of 10. The two numbers describe different things: a star rating clustered near the ceiling, and a review score that actually moves with what people wrote.
p5.s4_title: What people actually complained about (reviews are 2018–2021)
p5.s4_sub: Complaint categories pulled from the written reviews, sized by how often they appear and coloured by how much they drag the rating down
p5.chart_complaints_sub: x = number of reviews mentioning it · colour = average rating drag (grey = too few reviews to score)
p5.s4_insight: {{topShareLabel}} is the most common complaint ({{topShareN}} reviews, {{topSharePct}}% of all complaints) but only a mid-size drag. {{topDragLabel}} pulls the rating down hardest of any category — how often a complaint appears and how costly it is are two different things.
p5.s5_synthesis_title: So what actually moves the rating?
p5.s5_synthesis_sub: Tying the three findings above into one number worth acting on
p5.s5_synthesis_context: Ratings themselves barely separate one restaurant from another — half the comparable restaurants sit inside a band from {{p25}} to {{p75}} stars (median {{median}}). A rating this tight can't tell an owner or the platform which restaurant to fix.
p5.s5_synthesis_insight: {{nRestaurants}} of {{nReviewed}} reviewed restaurants name {{leadCategory}} as their #1 complaint — more restaurants than any other category. Fixing {{leadCategory}} first would reach more restaurants than a price move (section 01) or platform choice (section 02) ever could.
p5.s5_title: How this was collected, and what it does not show
p5.s5_sub: Method, the parse-only boundary, and the four things this dataset does not cover
p5.method_collect_text: A Python collector reads ShopeeFood's public Hanoi delivery listing and Foody's public review pages for the restaurants that appear on it, storing the star rating, category, price band, district, and the text of each written review.
p5.method_boundary_text: The collector only reads and stores pages that are already public. It never logs in, never places an order, and never posts, votes, or otherwise writes back to either site.
p5.method_ethics_text: Requests are rate-limited and restricted to public pages allowed by each site's robots.txt. No personal customer data is collected — only restaurant-level ratings, categories, and review text. Only the aggregates on this page are published; the raw snapshot never leaves local storage.
p5.method_accuracy_text: The complaint categories were assigned with Claude API assistance, then checked by hand on a 60-review re-read: {{pct}}% of those labels matched on review.
p5.method_notebook_link: View the analysis notebook on GitHub
caveats_items: This is the promoted, deliverable-to-one-address slice of the ShopeeFood Hanoi listing — not all of Hanoi.
The reviews run 2018–2021, not the present day.
Review coverage reaches {{reviewed}} of the {{total}} restaurants and skews toward the more popular ones.
The review count shown per restaurant is a display bucket ShopeeFood renders, not an exact count.
p5.method_note: Read every number on this page against those four points — a rating gap here is a gap in what was measurable, not necessarily a gap in the restaurant.
